reading.title: The Lemonade Experiment
reading.purpose: Follow two cousins who use numbers to settle a summer argument.
paras: Nikhil and his cousin Rosa ran a lemonade stand every summer, and every summer they argued about the same thing. Rosa said hot days made the best sales. Nikhil said it depended on the street. This year they decided to settle it with data. "We have to quantify it," Rosa said, writing a bold title on a clipboard. "Words like 'pretty good' are not numbers."

For twenty days they recorded the temperature at noon and the cups sold by six o'clock. The variation from day to day was huge. Some days they sold fewer than ten cups, and on others they sold almost forty. When Nikhil lined up the daily totals from smallest to largest, the median was twenty-two cups, which is the middle total on the list. "Half the days we sold less than that, and half more," he said.

One day stood out. On the afternoon of the street fair they sold ninety-one cups, far above every other day, so it was an outlier. "That day does not tell us anything about a normal Tuesday," Rosa said, and she marked it with a star. When they plotted the other totals on a graph, the distribution looked like a ramp, with a few cool days at the low end and many warm days toward the top.

Next they compared sales with temperature. Warmer days almost always meant more cups, so the two sets of numbers had a strong correlation. Nikhil frowned. "That does not prove the heat is the only reason," he said. "Maybe more neighbors are home on warm weekend days." Rosa nodded and wrote the idea on the clipboard as something to test next summer.

To decide where to set up the stand, they also asked a sample of thirty neighbors where they liked to walk. They knocked on doors on three streets, not just their own, so the sample would be representative of the whole block. The answer was a significant surprise: far more people walked past the park than past the school. The next morning the stand moved to the park gate, and the cousins taped their graph above the cooler.

qs.q: In paragraph 3, the word "outlier" most nearly means
choices: a total that is lower than every other total
a total that sits exactly in the middle of the list
a value that is far away from the others in a set
a total that repeats on several days in a row
qs.why: The street-fair day was "far above every other day," which is what makes a value an outlier.

qs.q: Which sentence explains why the cousins asked neighbors on three streets?
choices: To decide where to set up the stand, they also asked a sample of thirty neighbors where they liked to walk.
They knocked on doors on three streets, not just their own, so the sample would be representative of the whole block.
The answer was a significant surprise: far more people walked past the park than past the school.
The next morning the stand moved to the park gate, and the cousins taped their graph above the cooler.
qs.why: Only this sentence gives the reason: asking on three streets, not just their own, made the sample match the whole block.

ev.text: They knocked on doors on three streets, not just their own, so the sample would be representative of the whole block.

qs.q: Why does Rosa mark the street-fair day with a star?
choices: It was unusual, so it would not show what a normal day looks like.
It was the day when the temperature reached its highest point of the summer.
It was the first day that the cousins recorded any data at all.
It was the day when they sold the fewest cups all summer long.
qs.why: She says the day tells nothing about "a normal Tuesday," so the star warns that it is not typical.

qs.q: Which statement best sums up the story?
choices: Hot weather is the only thing that matters when a person sells lemonade.
Numbers are less useful than opinions when two people disagree about a plan.
A stand should be placed on whichever street has the most houses on it.
Collecting and checking numbers helped the cousins settle an argument and make a better choice.
qs.why: The cousins turn an argument into numbers, question what the numbers mean, and use them to move the stand.

clues.text: Words like 'pretty good' are not numbers.
the middle total on the list
Warmer days almost always meant more cups
